Foreword
We are looking into an AI-native era. Between hype, billion-dollar deals, and the hunt for AGI,
current GenAI has, in many ways, the potential to optimize processes and activities and
support white-collar workers in their capabilities. And while many organizations are still
looking for relevant business cases and problems to solve with GenAI, AI excels especially in
areas where we have more data than humans can imagine—where simple queries don't do the
job anymore, and continuously evolving system landscapes are hard to adopt operationally.
Observability is such a domain. The systems we create today are more distributed, dynamic,
and complex than ever before and produce endless logs, metrics, and traces. Due to the cloud-
native nature of most systems today, nothing happens without other parts of the system
knowing it too, and often reacting to it. This can become visible and actionable in your
observability data if you not only rely on simple queries to operate your system, but also are
one step ahead, by including AI. A traditional observability, while foundational, is no longer
enough. We need intelligence embedded into the fabric of our operations.
This is where Observability in the AI-Native Era arrives as a guide, providing you with the
starting point to include AI in your operational landscape. As long as I have known them, the
authors don't just like to theorize; they draw from decades of experience. They walk you
through how to integrate AI into your existing workflows through real-world case studies.
You'll see how AIOps moves beyond hype to deliver measurable improvements in reliability,
efficiency, and developer experience. You'll learn how to build observability platforms that
don't just alert teams to failures but prevent them, and how to democratize these capabilities
so every engineer can access AI-driven insights without becoming a data scientist.
The shift to AI-native observability isn't just technical, it's organizational. It challenges us to
redefine what "operational excellence" means in an era where systems can learn, adapt, and
even anticipate problems. The authors tackle these challenges head-on, offering frameworks

Preface
Over the past several years, the way we design, build, and operate software has shifted
dramatically. Modern systems are no longer monolithic, predictable, or even entirely human-
driven. Cloud-native architectures, internal developer platforms, and increasingly autonomous
AI components have reshaped the software lifecycle into something far more dynamic—and
far more complex. Amid this transformation, observability has emerged as one of the most
critical capabilities for engineering teams. Yet as telemetry grows and AI becomes a first-class
citizen in our stacks, the strategies that once served us well are no longer enough.
This book was written for engineers and leaders navigating that reality.
Whether you are a platform engineer improving developer workflows, a site reliability
engineer ensuring resilience, a DevOps engineer optimizing operations, or an engineering
leader striving to elevate operational excellence across teams, this book meets you where you
are. You do not need to be an expert in AI or observability to start. If you are working on or
moving toward an internal developer platform, books such as Platform Engineering for Architects

How can you prove the value of observability? It's not about capturing more data; it's about
turning this data into information that allows your organization to make better-informed
decisions about running your business more efficiently!
In this first chapter, we will give you an overview of everything we think you need to know
about observability, including its history and how it has evolved from monitoring. We will
discuss how to prove the value of observability and justify any investment into a modern
observability strategy. We will also explain the importance of high-quality observability data
as this is needed to successfully implement AIOps!
Be prepared to go on a journey through monitoring, learning how it has always helped IT
operations to keep the lights on. You will learn how observability emerged from monitoring as
we started to build more dynamic hybrid cloud-native distributed systems. Today, it's not just
about keeping the lights on; it's about using observability to run systems more cost-effectively,
enabling your software to become a competitive differentiator—and, with that, increasing
business output. We will also discuss the new roles within an organization that have emerged
over the years that benefit from idx_e07e8bc5 observability and Artificial Intelligence (AI). This includes
business leaders, developers, Site Reliability Engineers (SREs), observability idx_1057924f experts, and
platform engineers.

What is observability?
" Who needs observability anyway? I heard it's very expensive for the value it delivers, and we can
probably live without it! " This is a idx_ff43ab8c very common opinion that you'll encounter if you read
through online forums such as Reddit, Stack Overflow, or LinkedIn.
Indeed, proving the value of a project—whether it's around observability, AI, or Machine
Learning (ML) is idx_0f348867 a challenge.
Back in 2016, Gartner defined the term AIOps as referring " to the application of machine learning
and big data analytics to automate and enhance IT operations."
Initially, AIOps was about fixing the observability tool sprawl problem seen in many large
enterprises. AIOps was about leveraging AI and ML to correlate all signals from various
observability data sources to reduce alert noise. The value proposition of AIOps was to support
IT operations by identifying the root cause of IT problems faster in very complex hybrid-cloud
enterprise environments. While the promise of AIOps was great, the challenge for the initial

occur. The advancements in observability and AI can give AIOps the necessary intelligence to
move from the initial denoising of individual alerts to really connecting the dots of all

What is observability and how does it differ from
monitoring?
If you ask, " What is observability, what does it do, and how is it different from monitoring? " you will
likely idx_c6275496 get different idx_c45fae41 answers depending on people's backgrounds and experiences.
Let's ask ChatGPT!
As this book is about both observability and how AI can help organizations advance their
observability practice to improve software delivery and operations, let's put AI to the test. If we

search engines, we will get an answer similar to this:
"Observability is a characteristic of a system that allows you to understand its
internal state by examining its external outputs, like logs, metrics, and traces.
Monitoring, on the other hand, is the process of collecting predefined metrics and
thresholds to track system health. Observability is more proactive and investigative,
enabling you to understand why issues occur, while monitoring is more reactive,
alerting you to issues after they happen."
Google Search Lab – July 22, 2025
The early days: monitoring static systems
Not a bad definition at all that we received from our AI bot. The definition also highlights how
observability has emerged from monitoring. When looking back to the late 1990s and early
2000s—the early days of monitoring for some of us authors—monitoring was typically done
on predefined, well-known metrics, such as CPU, memory, garbage collection, disk utilization,
network bandwidth, package drop rate, service response times, and database connection pool
utilization. The next step was to specify meaningful thresholds to get alerted on when a metric
was reaching a known (or sometimes made-up) critical threshold value; for example, CPU
utilization greater than 90%, free disk space less than 5%, or TCP package loss greater than 1%.
Monitoring solutions were able to pull in metrics from the OS (using Linux system commands
or Windows performance counters) or via standards such as Simple Network Management
Protocol (SNMP). To idx_9efabee1 monitor business applications, it was possible to either pull process
metrics from the OS or leverage interfaces such as the idx_00444b9b popular Java Management Extension
(JMX) that allowed idx_1b4dcfa5 querying Java runtime and application-specific idx_1164ef84 metrics, such as garbage
collection, thread count, and memory utilization.
As systems were more static in nature, it was easy to maintain Configuration Management
Databases (CMDBs) with idx_e495c92d all of the details about your hosts, processes, and services.

The dawn of more complex and dynamic systems
This traditional idx_bb6ba2f5 approach to monitoring worked really well for the rather idx_994e62a2 static systems with a
manageable, well-defined set of health indicators. The limitations became apparent as IT
systems became more dynamic and complex in nature. Over the past years, many IT experts in
the industry have done the following:
Moved from a handful of physical servers to an idx_f51c5016 x-fold of Virtual Machines (VMs)
Refactored their old monolithic apps into many new microservices
Deployed multiple pods per service across availability zones or regions
Implemented business features using serverless idx_406a8749 or Web Assembly (WASM) technology
Migrated workloads from on-premises to the cloud or hybrid cloud
Released features dynamically using feature flagging
Integrated with a broad range of SaaS-based API offerings
The new variety of technologies also required new ways to monitor those systems and
runtimes. For some, it was no longer possible to simply install monitoring software or query
OS stats directly. Hypervisors (VMware), cloud vendors (AWS, Azure, and Google), and
Software as a Service (SaaS) vendors (Salesforce, Atlassian, SAP, and Workday) often
provided their idx_845ce97e own built-in monitoring solutions with basic dashboards and alerts. An
alternative approach was providing a proprietary interface to extract some of the metrics or
logs into your own monitoring solution, for example, the AWS CloudWatch API or Atlassian's
Monitoring API!

The challenges with those proprietary APIs were often around the lack of granularity of data,
the lack of standards that resulted in a lot of effort to query and parse the data, as well as the
additional costs that were charged by those vendors for using those APIs, including the
network traffic it took to get the data back to the in-house monitoring solution.
Cloud-native monitoring doesn't scale the way we need it to
When Google donated Kubernetes to the Linux Foundation, we not only saw the birth of the
Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) but idx_46ecfef2 also a boost in what idx_b9e08b84 we call cloud-native
architectures. Cloud native is not limited to running software on public cloud infrastructure;
it's a set of architectural principles that has led to hundreds, if not thousands, more
components that get developed dynamically rather than statically across public, private, or

We also deal with many new types and layers of systems that all provide lots of additional

are the days when a single metric could be combined with a static threshold to alert on a
healthy or unhealthy state. To visualize the new complexity of modern cloud-native systems,

With the idx_b2ac7504 ever-growing idx_cc52b463 complexity of the systems and the explosion of observability data, we
need a new way to turn this data into actionable information that doesn't require us to hire
and train hundreds of new experts!
AIOps 2.0: observability ready for the cloud-native AI era
Monitoring was idx_b80821f5 great for static systems with static thresholds that one could maintain in a
spreadsheet with clearly defined calls to action to remediate an isolated problem. Because our
systems have become so complex and dynamic, monitoring has to evolve into observability,
and we need automation and AI to cope with all this data to allow operators to make faster,
automated decisions.
AIOps 2.0 (for lack of a better term) has the chance to fulfill the initial promise of AIOps from
2016. To cope with the complexity and explosion of data, a cloud-native AI era observability
implementation requires the following:
Automated discovery of system components and their relationship, instead of
manually tracking hosts, processes, or services in a CMDB
Automatic baselining instead of manually setting thresholds on hundreds of
thousands of metrics
Automated anomaly detection that factors in seasonality, Service-Level Objectives
(SLOs), and idx_e5a6bac0 dependencies between system components
Automated root cause analysis that correlates abnormal signals based on end-to-end
system dependencies
Automated remediation that triggers and validates actions to keep a system in a
healthy state
As the complexity of our systems keeps growing exponentially, we also see the amount of data
growing at the same rapid pace. To make sense of all this data, observability needs smarter
algorithms and not to only look at data points in isolation. We need to look to ML and AI to
detect anomalies faster, understand the impact across highly dynamic and connected system
components, and use this data to speed up the remediation of the root cause to keep business
impact low. We must also leverage generative AI and LLMs to explain a situation and a
detected problem in a human-understandable way. The power of those systems is that they
have been trained on the global knowledge base created by experts over the years and shared
on the internet, for example, Stack Overflow and Reddit. That allows generative AI and LLMs to
help IT system operators to become more efficient while systems get more complex. Industry
vendors as well as analysts have coined the term AIOps, which talks about applying ML and AI
to support IT operations by making better decisions based on a large amount of observability
data.

By now, you should have a good understanding of monitoring and how it was focused on
understanding and alerting on the health status of static systems that we operated in the late
90s and early 2000s. With the move toward more dynamic, complex, and cloud-native
architectures, we needed a new approach to determine the health of our systems and identify
and fix the root cause quickly to limit any potential business impact. This is where modern
observability comes into play.

So far, we have only talked and given examples about metrics. However, metrics are just one of
the three well-known idx_61a5dac5 observability pillars. In the following idx_ac12349b section, we idx_458ded4f will explore all signals
that are relevant to modern observability. We will talk about emerging standards that make it
easier to collect this data and discuss some best practices for extracting information from each

Three pillars and beyond: use cases for logs, metrics, and
traces
In our brief introduction, we idx_c194e858 only glanced at some observability data examples around metrics,
such as CPU usage, memory consumption, garbage collection, service response time, and
network packet loss rate.
Observability, however, is more than metrics. The observability community typically talks
about the three pillars of observability: logs, metrics, and traces.
Thanks to innovation in the observability space, especially driven by open standards,
development framework and runtime developers, as well as observability platform vendors,
we see additional useful signals as telemetry data emerging that enable a lot of new use cases.
Here are some examples:
Events: Kubernetes events, continuous integration builds, or GitOps Deployment
events
Real user behavior: Opening a mobile app, reloading a frame, or changing screen
orientation
Code profiling: Detailed Java or .NET stack traces

detecting misconfiguration that leads to noncompliance with regulatory frameworks

11 Observability: The Art of Turning Data into Insights
While you might idx_d41a94dd already be familiar with individual signals, let's start with a quick
introduction to the pillars.
What are metrics?
Metrics are idx_6ef35fde numerical idx_638cb4cb data that we can capture from well-known entities such as network
devices, servers, processes, databases, or applications. Metrics typically present the current
state of the monitored entities, such as CPU usage, memory consumption, service response
time, and service failure rates. When continuously capturing those metrics, it helps us

understand system behavior over time. Metrics are typically used to set up alerting, for
example, to warn about a high failure rate of an application. Performance engineers and SREs
use metrics to optimize a system for better throughput, performance, or cost efficiency. For
example, they might increase the number of worker threads idx_ca6ff41f in a Java Virtual Machine (JVM)
to handle more concurrent requests.
The key challenges with metrics include high cardinality of metric dimensions, potential
privacy concerns with dimension names, large data volume and noise, as well as the overhead
of collecting, transporting, and analyzing metrics in real time.
Challenge: being careful with high cardinality and privacy in
dimensional data
Avoid the following common idx_847ca91f mistake: to identify suspicious activities from particular users or
IP addresses of an application, a developer can easily create a request count metric with the
dimensions username and IP address. While creating this metric is easy, analyzing it presents
challenges:
The backend data store needs to deal with potentially billions of unique IP addresses,
which makes it hard to calculate or alert on abnormal behavior for each unique IP
address
It allows everyone in your organization to view all usernames through access to a
technical metric, such as request count, which often poses a privacy concern
There is much more to learn about the proper creation and handling of metrics that we will
cover throughout the book, but idx_55a462d3 there are also many online resources that provide information
on different types of metrics, metric value aggregation, dimensions, and more.

What are logs?
Logs are idx_58334dad structured idx_45748890 or unstructured data that are created from similar entities that we can
capture metrics from, such as network devices, OSs, databases, or applications. Logs are
probably the oldest observability signal. If you have ever developed any type of code, you have
probably used a print or console.log statement. Initially, logs were used for troubleshooting,
allowing developers to better understand how their code executed on a remote system and
what transactions/requests were executed to understand where things failed. When analyzing
logs, developers often look for errors or exception stack traces, or for additional debug
information that was added to their code to make troubleshooting easier.
Logs have evolved a lot since the early days of software engineering. Today, most logging
frameworks used by developers produce structured log output with a set of standard fields,
such as timestamp (when the log was created), log level (ERROR, WARNING, INFO, or DEBUG),
context (request ID, application ID, etc.), and the content (the actual log message). Logs,
typically captured and enriched through agents such as Fluentd, Logstash, or OpenTelemetry
(OpenTel), are also idx_1963bf99 typically sent through a log pipeline, which enriches the log with even
more context, such as log source, server, or Kubernetes cluster, namespace, or Pod.
Challenge: tackling high-volume, excessive, and unstructured logs
While there are several idx_42b1cd22 challenges with logs, the top challenge is that systems tend to produce
high volumes of logs, and not every log line is relevant for daily operations. As many
organizations operate a lot of software that has been around for a while, chances are also very
high that many logs are unstructured and therefore hard to analyze. Because it's easy to create
logs, we often see excessive logging by applications that can't be controlled easily. A common
mistake is adding but never removing debug logs that were needed for a quick troubleshooting
session.
Because of the high volume of logs across most software systems, logs are often considered
very expensive. While this is true, one must not blame the observability backend as a first
response. Logs are important, but it requires a good logging culture and automated checks to
keep logs under control.
There is much more we will learn about proper log management throughout this book, such as
extracting metrics out of logs and storing only those logs that are relevant for critical use cases,
for example, compliance idx_6ec8570b and security. As with metrics, please also consult the many online
resources available on structured logging and log pipelines.
13 Observability: The Art of Turning Data into Insights
What are traces?
Distributed idx_80674d9a traces are the youngest of the pillars. A distributed idx_078a8e2b trace tracks a single request as it

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 1 12
chunks.content:
flows through multiple services in a distributed system, providing insights into the request's
journey and performance across different components.
They were introduced in the idx_e3e80d0c early 2000s by Application Performance Management (APM)
vendors such as Wily (now part of Broadcom), Dynatrace, AppDynamics (now part of Cisco),
and New Relic. Initially focusing on Java and .NET, the agents of those vendors were able to
instrument byte code when it was loaded by the JVM/.NET runtime. With this approach, no
manual code changes were necessary. The automated distributed trace output gave developers
an end-to-end view, starting from a web request entering the web or application server,
moving through queues or middleware, and continuing to the backend services and finally the
database.
The distributed trace was not only a great debugging tool for developers to understand
dynamic code execution in distributed systems, but was also often integrated into performance
testing and later production environments to understand the performance and load behavior
of individual components.
The big challenge that distributed tracing had to solve was the propagation of the unique trace
ID from the first service to the last. This was typically done via HTTP headers, message
properties, or by passing it through thread-local storage in multi-threaded code.
What used to require proprietary instrumentation and data formats has recently been
standardized through the CNCF project OpenTel. The following visualization shows the
anatomy of an end-to-end trace captured through OpenTel. Each trace has a unique ID. Every
piece of information captured, such as a web request, database calls, or method invocation, is
represented as a so-called span. Spans have a relation to a parent span and to the trace they
belong to.

the Unleash the Power of Distributed Traces YouTube video [1]. We also cover more aspects of

Challenge: over-instrumentation, duplicated data, and sampling as
challenges
Over the past 20 years, vendors idx_76e1fe52 have optimized their agents to avoid over-instrumentation
(capturing too many calls or too much information), reduce the collection of duplicated data
(same data as part of a trace and part of a log), and optimize their sampling strategies
(deciding what data to store and what to filter out).
As many organizations try to reduce their dependencies on vendor agents, they are shifting the
responsibility of instrumenting code to their developers. While OpenTel is maturing and more
developer tools exist that support engineers with their instrumentation, the challenges of
over-instrumentation, duplicated idx_7fd46085 data, and proper sampling decisions need to be taken into
consideration for every observability project looking into distributed tracing.
15 Observability: The Art of Turning Data into Insights
Beyond the three pillars: use cases based on events, profiling,
and real users
Besides logs, metrics, and idx_cc9b4ef4 traces, we have additional observability signals that enable
additional use cases and benefits for roles such as DevOps engineers, platform engineers, line-
of-business leaders, security teams, architects, and developers. The following are some real-life
examples and use cases based on runtime or life cycle events, real user monitoring, code
profiling, and security insights.
Use case: track your software development life cycle through events
" Where is my build? How long does it take to get a code fix into production? Which Git commit just
broke production? " These and similar questions can be answered by using observability to track
the life cycle of your code and build artifacts from the first Git commit through your
continuous integration, testing, continuous delivery, and finally release into production.
The OpenTel community has started to standardize semantic conventions for observability
data from CI/CD systems to make this easier. Vendors such as Dynatrace have started to define
Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) events to track an artifact by ingesting
observability idx_e3e877bd data from tools such as Jira, GitHub, GitLab, Azure DevOps, Argo CD, and Flux.
Tracking artifacts through observability not only gives you the chance to report on efficiency
metrics such idx_64dcd4cc as DevOps Research and Assessment (DORA) but also allows you to provide

chunks.heading: Chapter 1 14
chunks.content:
more context to your AIOps system for better root cause detection of a problem. When
implemented, it allows you to automatically pinpoint the problematic pull request, Git
commit, or pipeline run that caused a production issue.
Use case: provide real-time business insights by extracting business
events
" What is the business impact of our latest feature rollout? Has the revenue increased since we enabled
our new AI chatbots for our premium users? Why does it take a week to get the updated business
impact report? " These are common questions that we hear from business leaders. The biggest
challenge is getting real-time business insights and understanding how technical changes
impact business outcomes, either positively or negatively. By using observability to monitor
logs, metrics, and traces from those business IT systems, we can typically extract business
events and use that to provide real-time business reporting and insights connected with the
technical data.

To give you an example, in an e-commerce platform, we can capture the shopping cart volume
either from logs or traces or by asking our developers to export a custom metric. Combined
with the additional context we have about the end user (such as their IP address range) and
whether they completed a purchase (successful execution of the purchase API endpoint), we
can provide real-time reporting about realized versus unrealized value by geographical region.
More use cases on existing observability signals
Throughout Chapter 3, we will provide more detailed use cases covering areas such as
optimizing user experience through real user behavior analytics, increasing developer
efficiency through code profiling and live debugging, assessing security attack and
vulnerability risks, and managing compliance by automatically validating mandatory
compliance requirements. These are all use cases that can be implemented today with our
existing observability signals!
Use cases: more to come as observability is evolving
What started decades ago with monitoring metrics and then expanded to logs and distributed
traces has now expanded into many more signals that have opened up new use cases, as
explained earlier. As the observability space keeps evolving, thanks to the emerging standards
and constant innovation in the space, there will be new use cases based on those existing
signals. It's also likely that new signals will emerge. Throughout this book, we will dive deeper
into more use cases, best idx_e97a6082 practices, and how organizations go about implementing them as
part of a modern observability strategy!
The next question we need to answer is: where does all this data come from? Are there any
standards or is this all done by proprietary implementations of a small handful of observability
vendors?
Emerging standards over the years
Early monitoring of idx_4ee5741c distributed systems focused on standard protocols such as SNMP or the
OS's built-in basic monitoring tools and interfaces to understand the health of the OS, the
running processes, and the utilization of the hardware it ran on.
Starting in the early 2000s, Application Performance Monitoring (APM) elevated basic
system monitoring idx_7a387743 to sophisticated, real-time, end-to-end observability into performance,
resiliency and execution behavior of distributed systems. APM vendors (Dynatrace,
AppDynamics, New Relic, Datadog, Instana, etc.) provided custom-built proprietary agents
that automatically captured metrics, logs, and traces on the systems (Linux or Windows) that
they were installed on. Moving from one vendor to another wasn't an easy task as there were
no real standards on both data collection and analysis that made switching easy.

This probably also idx_864e2cf0 resulted in vendor lock-in as one of the top arguments that organizations
bring up when advocating for new open standards for modern observability. With the dawn of
cloud-native architectures, especially around Kubernetes, we have seen several emerging
standards driven by the open source community to standardize the way to collect, transform,
and analyze observability data in modern cloud-native distributed systems.
Let's provide a quick overview of the most important standards and open source projects.
OpenTelemetry
The most prominent idx_1bc4010c of these standards is the CNCF project OpenTel [2]: an idx_33bcb167 open source
observability framework and toolkit designed to facilitate the generation, export, and
collection of traces, metrics, and logs. In 2019, OpenTel emerged from the merger of
OpenCensus and OpenTracing and has recently started to expand into more signals, such as
code profiling and real user monitoring.
While OTel is not an observability backend for storing and analyzing data, this standard has
opened up a lot of innovation across the full spectrum of observability:
Instrumentation: The community, as well as vendors, contribute to auto-
instrumentation agents for various runtimes and languages.
Collection: The OpenTel Collector provides a vendor-agnostic way to receive, process,
and export telemetry data. The community and vendors provide a huge range of
extensions, making the OTel Collector a great observability data pipeline.
Analysis: By commoditizing the collection of observability data, many new open
source tools and vendors emerged, providing analysis capabilities on pure OpenTel
data.
A key component in an OpenTel implementation is the OpenTel Collector [3]. The following
screenshot is taken from the OpenTel website, highlighting its extensible architecture around
receivers (pulling in data from various data sources), processors (normalizing, sampling,
extracting, or enriching data), and exporters (sending it to the storage and analysis
observability backends).

When implementing OpenTel as a data receiver and pipeline, please be aware of the constantly

Most commercial observability platforms support OpenTel, either by supporting the

19 Observability: The Art of Turning Data into Insights
Prometheus
Prometheus [4], initially idx_ccdca534 developed at SoundCloud idx_3d4936d4 starting in 2012, is another very popular
open source monitoring and alerting system. It was created to address limitations of existing
monitoring solutions at the time, particularly around multi-dimensional data models, scalable
data collection, and a simple yet powerful query language called PromQL. Prometheus joined
the CNCF in 2016 and graduated as a project in 2018. Compared to OpenTel, Prometheus
focuses on gathering metrics that get stored in a time-series database optimized for high-
cardinality, which makes it a good choice for real-time monitoring and historical trend
analysis. Metrics can be enriched with additional context in the form of key-value pairs, which
address some of the challenges we discussed earlier, which is enriching metrics with
information about their origin, as well as additional business data dimensions.
The key architectural components are as follows:
Exporting metrics: Services idx_eb3780b5 need to export metrics via an HTTP endpoint that gets
scraped by Prometheus. The community provides many existing exporters for various
systems, frameworks, or APIs (for example, Apache, Nginx, Kafka, or BIG-IP).
Developers can also export their own metrics using the available client libraries for the
various programming languages.
Ingesting metrics: The Prometheus server scrapes a set of configured endpoints
(applications, servers, etc.) on a periodic interval by sending HTTP requests to those
targets. It expects the endpoint to return the requested metrics, their metric type, and

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 1 18
chunks.content:
their values.
Storing metrics: The Prometheus server provides a local on-disk time-series database
for storing ingested metrics, but can also optionally integrate with remote storage
systems.
Alerting: Alerting rules in Prometheus servers send alerts to the Alertmanager. The
Alertmanager then manages those alerts, including silencing, inhibition, aggregation,
and sending out notifications via methods such as email, on-call notification systems,
and chat platforms.
Visualization: Prometheus is commonly used with Grafana, an open source analytics
and visualization platform, to visualize and analyze Prometheus metrics and alerts on
dashboards. As most observability platforms (open source and commercial) integrate idx_f5e457f2
with Prometheus, you are not limited to Grafana.
Prometheus is widely adopted, and thanks to the wide array of available exporters, most
modern software components provide automatic Prometheus metrics that can be scraped by a
Prometheus server or an OpenTel Collector, or directly from your commercial observability
platform.

In a modern observability strategy, Prometheus will most likely play a key role in observing
metrics. Make sure to idx_85442605 look into all the best practices that the idx_701dd1e0 community suggests around
setup, scale, and integrations. We will also provide more examples and guidance throughout
this book on how to integrate Prometheus into your enterprise observability strategy.
Visualization standards: Grafana and Perses
Grafana is a very popular idx_34885d1a open source platform used to idx_08925b1d visualize idx_3f31b2e2 and analyze various types of
observability data from various sources. Grafana is the default visualization tool for
Prometheus metrics, and you will find lots of pre-configured dashboards for various system
components (for example, Kubernetes, MongoDB, Kafka, and AWS) that the community has
created and maintained. Grafana is created by Grafana Labs, which also provides commercial
products on top of their various open source projects.
While there is no shortage of available Grafana dashboards, the dashboard file format is not
standardized, which makes it hard to leverage Grafana dashboards with other observability
visualization solutions. The open source project Perses is set to address this problem by
providing an open specification for dashboards for Prometheus and other data sources. Perses
is currently a CNCF sandbox project but has already been adopted by several observability
vendors, as well as end user companies, based on information the Perses website [5].
Standardizing the way data gets displayed, analyzed, and alerted on is the next step toward
providing a vendor-neutral definition for observability. While OpenTel and Prometheus have
done a good job of reducing the vendor lock-in argument on the data collection side, Perses
aims to do the same for visualizing the data.
By now, you have a good understanding of how observability has emerged out of monitoring.
We have discussed the different signals of observability that go beyond logs, metrics, and
traces. We have touched upon emerging standards to collect and visualize data and have
discussed the need to leverage automation, AI, and ML to fully harness the growing amount of
data to better support all the teams that require observability data to make better and faster
decisions. But we are just at the start of our journey. Next, we will look into one of the biggest
challenges that modern idx_272a2d36 observability solves: understanding idx_b734f801 distributed idx_247d2d59 systems.
Observability and distributed systems
In this section, we want idx_5784ff56 to dive into distributed systems and the idx_68a3477a critical role observability plays
as our systems become more complex.
For starters, it feels odd to call out "a distributed system" because any system that is not

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 1 20
chunks.content:
exclusively running on a single host or server is, by definition, a distributed system. That has
been true for many decades since we escaped the monolithic systems of the early days of the
mainframe. One could also argue that even then, we had a distributed system because code
21 Observability: The Art of Turning Data into Insights
execution and data storage were decoupled; hence, we could also talk about a distributed
system that was able to execute business functions.
Highly distributed systems and the increased complexity
What has drastically idx_52a54a49 changed in recent years is the number of components involved in a
distributed system, the distribution of those components across different platforms and
locations, the additional layers of abstraction between the hardware and the code that
executes business logic, as well as the dynamic elasticity when we look at the deployment
models. All of this makes the management of those highly distributed systems more complex.
What used to be a handful of physical servers became an X-fold of VMs running on physical
servers. What used to be many VMs running on a handful of physical machines turned into an
X-fold of elastic cloud compute instances (for idx_8a284ff3 example, AWS Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2)
instances in various sizes). If we idx_12b2b41f look into cloud-native architectures, we see another X-fold in
the number of pods or serverless functions deployed on-premises or in the cloud, orchestrated
through platforms such as Kubernetes, OpenShift, or any of the hyperscaler-provided
workflow services. The advances in deployment orchestration and auto-scaling have also
increased the frequency of changes. Deployments that used to be done monthly or weekly are
now fully automated and can happen multiple times a minute. These changes can range from
deploying a new workload or right-sizing existing ones to cope with increased demand to
moving workloads to different data center regions to optimize performance or cost, or
switching feature flags to control the behavior of applications and services.
Understanding distributed systems through observability
As somebody responsible for idx_67d75fab a distributed system, you need to be able to answer a handful of
key questions around inventory, dependencies, APIs, health, SLAs, and root cause.
Observability can help you answer all these questions, allowing you to better understand,
better manage, and, with that, better operate your distributed systems.
In the next sections, we walk through these questions with examples and give you some
guidance on how you should go about answering those questions to validate how mature your
observability strategy already is.

Inventory: which components are part of the system we are
responsible for?
We need a list of hosts, network devices, Kubernetes nodes, cloud infrastructure, processes,
pods, serverless functions, and databases. With observability, we get insights into the systems
we actively monitor (for example, through Prometheus or an observability agent). It also
allows us to discover components that we are not actively monitoring, for instance, by
analyzing network connections from a monitored host to other IP addresses or by querying a
discovery API from the cloud provider or the orchestration platform.
Later in the book, we will walk through best practices on how to roll out observability, discover
blind spots, and increase observability coverage.
Dependencies: how are components connected and dependent
on each other?
We need to know the vertical dependencies (which components connect to each other via a
network) and horizontal dependencies (which components run on other components, for
example, processes running on hosts). This helps us to understand, for instance, which
processes share the same CPU or connect to the same database.
Metrics, logs, and traces that are enriched with metadata about the system where they are
captured automatically tell us the vertical dependencies. For example, the CPU usage of a
process includes information about the host it is running on. Monitoring network connections
as well as distributed tracing additionally tells us the horizontal dependencies, since it
contains the information of which system communicates with which other system.
Interfaces/APIs: what are the boundaries of our distributed
system to the consumers?
We need to know critical endpoints (HTTP, messaging, and so on) that need to be available and
accessible by our users or third-party consumers. These endpoints can additionally be
monitored through synthetic checks to ensure availability.
Observability can help us automatically detect endpoints by extracting this information from
our network traffic logs or distributed traces, or by querying the information from exposed
endpoints on load balancers and ingress definitions.
Health: are all components working as expected or is there
abnormal behavior?
We need to know how to determine the health status of any component to understand
whether a component is a potential root cause of an incident.
23 Observability: The Art of Turning Data into Insights
Observability helps us ingest logs, metrics, traces, and events from our components. We can
then set up health alerts such as high CPU usage, database connection timeouts, service failure
rate, critical error logs, or slower-than-usual service response time. The latter is an example of
automated baselining, whereas the former is often done through static thresholds.

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 1 22
chunks.content:
A key consideration must be not managing hundreds or thousands of alert thresholds
manually but using defaults for known health indicators, along with automated baselines and
machine learning, to keep the management overhead to a minimum.
We will cover many idx_caf257b0 examples later in the book about how to best set up health monitoring and
alerting on abnormal behavior.
SLA and root cause: are end-to-end critical transactions
experiencing issues, and why?
We need to get alerted in case our critical transactions are unavailable, not returning accurate
results, or not performing as expected to avoid potential impacts on idx_8fb5547f our Service-Level
Agreements (SLAs).
Observability doesn't just help us with being alerted when a problem is already occurring. The
goal with a modern observability implementation is to get alerted before we breach our SLAs.
This can be done by leveraging AI on all the observability signals, including the contextual
information about which components are involved in the critical end-to-end transactions. If
one of these components starts acting abnormally, a remediation action can be triggered to
mitigate the situation before it impacts the whole of the system.
Later in this book, we will cover lots of examples and best practices on how to leverage AI and
observability to move from reactive to proactive to preventative operations.

Component health: A Linux host is having issues that are impacting the services that
are running on it. We can get this information by setting up alerts on key OS metrics
such as CPU, memory, disk, and network, as well as alerts on service metrics such as

What was already apparent in this section was that distributed systems have a lot of

Shared infrastructure and how it impacts components
In a distributed idx_8ff83500 system, we idx_8d8942b3 have a lot of shared infrastructure—whether that is the shared CPU
and memory across all Pods on a Kubernetes node, the VMs that fight for the same hardware of
the underlying physical server, or the individual processes on a Linux OS that share the same
disks they want to read/write to.
From an observability perspective, it's important that we understand what infrastructure is
available and who is using that infrastructure. This allows us to answer a lot of important
questions, such as " Do we have a noisy neighbor that impacts other services? " and opens up a lot of
interesting use cases, such as " Can we optimize resource utilization to save costs? " Besides ITOps

and SREs, we see FinOps teams leveraging observability to optimize costs while keeping an eye
on not negatively impacting critical components that are needed to ensure business objectives
are met.

When ingesting logs, metrics, or traces, it's important that those signals get enriched

Use case: identifying a noisy neighbor
If you've ever lived in an apartment with roommates where you also had to share a bathroom,
and maybe had thin walls where you could hear every word spoken on the other side, you
understand the noisy neighbor problem.
The same problem exists with shared infrastructure. Classic examples are VMs, processes, or
pods that use excessive CPU, memory, network, or disk on a shared host or node. This behavior
will impact all other processes. It will slow them down or even cause them to crash or not start
at all. The problem typically happens if there are idx_3bede489 no guardrails specified around how much
memory or CPU a pod can use, for example, by specifying request and resource limits.
Figure 1.7: Identifying noisy neighbors requires detailed observability of all key metrics (CPU, memory, disk, etc.)
per consumer (VM, process, pod, etc.)
It's a good practice to keep an eye on noisy neighbors not only when trying to identify root
causes but also to idx_5a20e862 identify idx_2f888c11 missing guardrails on certain deployments. One alert to set up
would be if individual processes constantly use more than 10 times the resources (CPU,
memory, disk, etc.) than their neighbors. This is a good indicator to take action.
Use case: right-sizing infrastructure based on real needs
Let's stay with our roommate analogy. Imagine you have an apartment with five bedrooms, yet
you only use one room. That's a very large and probably costly apartment to maintain. The
same is true for shared infrastructure. If you constantly have idle resources, it's a sign to reduce
the size of the underlying shared infrastructure. This is more efficient and also saves costs. Talk
with your FinOps department; they would be happy to get automated reports from
observability with a list of resources that are not well utilized and can be downsized.
The opposite scenario is also possible: constant high utilization. You can use observability to
analyze whether this increase in demand for the services that run on this shared infrastructure

is constant or just seasonal. If there is a constant increase in service utilization (for example, an
increased number of requests to that service over the past months), then either increase the
size of the underlying shared infrastructure or consider moving this workload to a better-sized
home.
From shared infrastructure, it's only a small step to shared communication. Distributed
systems only work because components communicate via different means. Let's dive into the
role of observability idx_157303e9 for idx_76f1bc6f synchronous and asynchronous communication!
Synchronous and asynchronous communication
We discussed that idx_cd5f894b distributed idx_d88ec1b0 tracing is a great way to identify how services communicate

with each other, as trace technology can follow a transaction from the end user (browser or
mobile device) through all the middleware and microservices to the backend databases. This
works by propagating the idx_8baef40d so-called trace context via the communication protocol (HTTP,
messaging, etc.) from the service caller to the callee. We covered this topic in more detail
earlier in this chapter.
From an observability perspective, a distributed trace is not always enough to fully understand
whether there is a communication problem between two components. The trace will contain
timestamps from the outgoing call on the caller and the incoming call on the callee. But what if
the difference between those two timestamps varies a lot? What if it is 10 milliseconds on one
trace and 10 seconds on the next? And what if some traces show a timeout error and the call
never reaches the callee? What might be the reason for this slowdown or failure?
Observability also has a solution to answer these questions as we need to expand observability
into the layers of the architecture that make synchronous and asynchronous communication
possible. We are talking about the network, connections, and queues. All those layers also need
to be observed to get the full picture of what is happening in distributed communication.
Network: metrics or eBPF
Most communication happens via the network, whether this is on the same host or across
continents. Observability can give us insights into the network layer around traffic (bytes and
packets sent and received), quality (packet errors or dropped packets), and connectivity
(number of sessions and timed-out sessions). These metrics are typically readily available from
the OS as well as network devices.
A new player on the field is idx_f153e658 the extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF), with Cilium being idx_173e6c84
the prominent open source project that uses eBPF to provide insights into network
connectivity between workloads. The online communities provide a lot to learn about eBPF,
and we will also cover it in other use cases later in this book. What is important to know is that
eBPF provides an additional way to answer the question: Is it the network or not?

Connections: pools on each side of the call
When two services communicate with each other, each side (also referred to as the client and
server) typically opens a connection to then send messages. To better manage those
connections and avoid the need to open a new connection every time, we have the concept of
connection pools. Connection idx_45cc25c2 pools manage open connections that can then be requested
when needed, used to make a call, and finally, returned to the pool for other requests to use.
Those connection pools exist in most frameworks to open connections to an HTTP or database
endpoint. Improperly sized connection pools and connection leaks are the most common
issues when a client and a server can't efficiently communicate. One is about having too many
concurrent requests for a connection, while the other one is about keeping a connection out of
the pool for longer than actually needed. Both scenarios mean that the next request that needs
a connection has to idx_b96ac0b3 wait idx_9908ed6b for one to become available in the pool.
Observability tip
If there are errors or slowdowns in communication, then it's advisable to analyze the
health of the network. It could be another noisy neighbor that is consuming all network
bandwidth or a faulty network component that drops packets. The answer lies in the
observability insights we get from the network layer.
Tip
Observability tip
Consult the documentation of the application runtimes and frameworks that your
developers use for cross-service communication. Those typically provide metrics
around pool size and pool usage. Pools that are constantly underutilized or fully
utilized are a sign of improper sizing or bad connection handling. Also, when adjusting
pool sizes, remember to adjust them appropriately on both sides where you have pools:
the client and the server.

Queues: the distributors of messages
RabbitMQ, Apache Kafka, Amazon SQS, Azure Service Bus, and Google Pub/Sub are some of the
prominent message queues used in distributed architectures. The concept is rather simple: you
have a sender pushing a message into the queue and a receiver pulling a message out to process
it. Queues allow decoupling of components as they become the intermediary between the
client and the server. Queues can also hold on to messages for a while until they are pulled,
which makes them perfect for smoothing out spike loads of new messages until the receivers
can process them.
Like the network and connection pools, queues provide good observability to understand
whether the queue is healthy and doing its job or whether it is the problem of a slow or failed
asynchronous communication.
Remember that queues will be present in almost every distributed architecture. They enable

alerting set up.
With OpenTel becoming more widely adopted, end-to-end synchronous and asynchronous
communication will be traceable through OTel. This is great news for everyone. Just remember
that there is always a component between the two ends of a communication, whether it's a
network, a connection pool, or a queue. These have to be observed as they are the backbone of
any communication in a distributed system.
Networks, connections, and queues enable easier communication between an ever-growing
number of components. Easier communication typically results in more components that take
part across those communication channels. Those are all components and infrastructure that
need to be managed. If you have managed dynamic infrastructure, you have probably heard
about the pets versus cattle analogy. To learn more about what this means for observability, we
Observability tip
Consult the documentation of the queue system you are using. Chances are there is an
existing Prometheus exporter, or it already provides OpenTel metrics or traces. Key
metrics that indicate health are queue length, message throughput, failed message
delivery rates, and the time messages spend in the queue. If queues are not properly
sized, or when too many messages are sent and not received, you will see an increase in
queue length, leading to an increase in the time messages spend in the queue. You can
also judge how stable a system performs by looking at message throughput and
delivery rates.

containers, and databases before we conclude by defining the focus of the rest of the book.
VMs, containers, and databases – oh my!
In modern IT systems, we find all sorts of technical components and services. In our
Observability and distributed systems section, we already covered how the evolution from VMs to
containers and beyond is impacting the way we approach observability.
Many organizations that operate IT systems today have a wide variety of existing web servers,
application servers, and databases, with some of those running on VMs, as containers, or even
as serverless functions. It's important to cover best practices and ways to observe those critical
components that operate the core system components of many enterprise organizations.
Observing hypervisors and VMs
When using VMs, it's important to observe both the VMs and the underlying hypervisor.
Whether that is idx_7bb4e694 VMware, Microsoft's Hyper-V, Citrix Hypervisor, VirtualBox, or idx_d2f23194 KVM, these
platforms typically provide their own observability tooling along with metrics that can be
ingested into a central observability platform. Key metrics to focus on here are the same as
what we discussed around shared infrastructure: CPU, memory, storage, and network. On top
of that, those hypervisors typically also provide some basic monitoring of the VMs that they
are orchestrating.
Observability best practice
While hypervisor monitoring gives you a good basic coverage of VMs, it's advisable to
get insights into what is happening on the VM itself. You want to know which processes
and services run on those VMs and who is consuming how many resources. Consult the
documentation from your observability platform. There typically exists an option either
by installing an agent or by querying those VM metrics through an extension, which
might pull the data through Prometheus, Windows Management Interface (WMI), or
other idx_e61c7240 data sources provided by the OS running in the VM.
